Using an Xbox Wireless Controller (Series X|S, USB‑C) with the official Microsoft USB dongle on Linux is not plug‑and‑play.
Unlike Bluetooth, the dongle requires runtime firmware and a user‑space daemon called xow.
This note documents the minimal, working setup that finally made it work.
Environment OS: Arch Linux (Omarchy) Kernel: 6.x Controller: Xbox Wireless Controller (Series X|S, USB‑C, Carbon Black) Dongle: Microsoft Xbox Wireless Adapter (045e:02fe) Desktop: Hyprland Games: Steam Controller Details Official product page:
https://www.xbox.com/en-US/accessories/controllers/xbox-wireless-controller-usb-c
Connection modes:
USB‑C (wired)
Xbox Wireless (2.4 GHz via official dongle)
The Problem Symptoms I hit:
Controller LED keeps blinking
Dongle visible in lsusb but will not pair
xow service crashes or restarts
Errors like:
Failed to load firmware
Firmware reset timed out
LIBUSB_ERROR_ACCESS
Sometimes the service looked active, but nothing actually worked.
Why This Happens xow is not a kernel driver.
It:
Runs in user space Talks to the dongle via libusb Uploads Microsoft firmware at runtime Emulates an Xbox controller for Linux input devices If firmware is missing or pairing order is wrong, the dongle stays unusable.
The Fix 1. Install xow git clone https://github.com/medusalix/xow.git cd xow make sudo make install 2. Install firmware (required) sed "s|@prefix@|/usr/local|g" install/firmware.sh.in > /tmp/xow-firmware.sh chmod +x /tmp/xow-firmware.sh sudo /tmp/xow-firmware.sh This installs:
/lib/firmware/xow_dongle.bin Verify:
ls -l /lib/firmware/xow_dongle.bin 3. systemd Service Configuration This is the working xow service file I ended up using.
[Unit] Description=Xbox One Wireless Dongle Driver [Service] Type=simple ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/xow Restart=on-failure Environment="XOW_COMPATIBILITY=1" [Install] WantedBy=multi-user.target Edit it with:
sudo SYSTEMD_EDITOR=nvim systemctl edit --full xow Enable and start:
sudo systemctl enable xow --now 4. Pair Using USB (Important) For Xbox Series X|S controllers, pairing once via USB is required.
Steps:
Plug controller using a USB‑C cable
Start xow
Wait for:
Dongle initialized Unplug the USB cable
Press pairing button on:
Dongle
Controller
After this, wireless pairing works normally.
Verify journalctl -u xow shows:
Dongle initialized
Pairing enabled
Controller LED becomes solid
Steam detects an Xbox Controller
Games receive input
Lessons Learned The official Xbox dongle requires firmware (xow or xone) xow is a user‑space USB translator, not a kernel driver USB pairing once is necessary for Series X|S controllers Linux exposes complexity that Windows hides TL;DR Install xow Install firmware Enable service Pair once via USB Use wireless after References xow: https://github.com/medusalix/xow Xbox Controller: https://www.xbox.com/en-US/accessories/controllers/xbox-wireless-controller-usb-c
summary: Using Xbox controller with official USB dongle required runtime firmware and user-space darmon called xow.
title: Fixing Xbox Series X|S Controller with official Dongle on Arch Linux (Omarchy)

Introduction I’ve been wanting to document my projects, my work, and the new things I learn by turning them into blog posts or shared personal notes. While I already have a lot of projects documented in my personal notes, I haven’t published much since I posted on Medium a couple of years ago.
I believe that sharing my personal projects and fun learning experiences will help improve my writing skills. In this blog post, I will show you how to turn your personal notes directly into published blog posts.
Tools that I use Over the years, I’ve used a variety of note-taking apps like Notion, Evernote, and Apple Notes. Recently, I switched to Obsidian, a markdown-based note app. It was easy to pick up since I already use Markdown for most of my personal and work projects.
My goal is to treat my notes as my “Second Brain.” I use the PARA method by Tiago Forte to organize my notes in Obsidian, which makes it incredibly easy to push them straight to my personal blog (ahmadfakhrozy.com).
To make the blog work, I use Hugo. Hugo is an open-source static site generator that easily converts Markdown into static HTML files. Plus, there are tons of great templates built by the community that you can use right out of the box.
Workflow flowchart LR A[Obsidian Posts] -->|rsync| B[Hugo Posts] C[Obsidian Attachments] -->|rsync| D[Hugo Images] B --> E[Convert Links] D --> F[Compress Images] E --> G[Hugo Build] F --> G G --> H[Git Push Main] My workflow starts with my posts and attachments in Obsidian. The script syncs them to the Hugo directory, converts the image links, and compresses the images. Then, it builds the site and pushes it to GitHub, where an automated CI pipeline publishes the static site via Netlify.
Everything is handled by a single Python sync script that I created. I will include the full script at the end of this post!
During my research, I noticed that NetworkChuck built a very similar automated Hugo pipeline. If you want a more detailed guide on setting up Hugo from scratch, I highly recommend checking out his article: My Insane Blog Pipeline.
#!/bin/bash set -euo pipefail # Change to the script's directory (hugo-blog root) SCRIPT_DIR="$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")" && pwd)" cd "$SCRIPT_DIR" # ============================================================================= # Script Options # ============================================================================= DRY_RUN=false BRANCH="${BRANCH:-main}" # Parse command line arguments while [[ $# -gt 0 ]]; do case $1 in --dry-run|-n) DRY_RUN=true echo "🏃 Dry-run mode enabled - no changes will be committed or pushed" shift ;; --help|-h) echo "Usage: ./sync.sh [OPTIONS]" echo "" echo "Options:" echo " --dry-run, -n Preview changes without committing or pushing" echo " --help, -h Show this help message" echo "" echo "Environment Variables:" echo " OBSIDIAN_POSTS Path to Obsidian posts folder" echo " OBSIDIAN_ATTACHMENTS Path to Obsidian attachments folder" echo " HUGO_POSTS Path to Hugo posts destination" echo " HUGO_IMAGES Path to Hugo images destination" echo " MYREPO GitHub repository URL" echo " BRANCH Git branch to push (default: main)" exit 0 ;; *) echo "Unknown option: $1" echo "Use --help for usage information" exit 1 ;; esac done # ============================================================================= # Configuration (can be overridden via environment variables) # edit the variable base of your directory and repo ============================================================================= # Obsidian paths OBSIDIAN_POSTS="${OBSIDIAN_POSTS:-...}" OBSIDIAN_ATTACHMENTS="${OBSIDIAN_ATTACHMENTS:-.....}" # Hugo paths HUGO_POSTS="${HUGO_POSTS:-...}" HUGO_IMAGES="${HUGO_IMAGES:-...}" # GitHub repo MYREPO="${MYREPO:-...}" # ============================================================================= # Pre-flight checks # ============================================================================= echo "🔍 Checking required commands..." for cmd in git rsync python3 hugo; do if ! command -v $cmd &> /dev/null; then echo "❌ $cmd is not installed or not in PATH." exit 1 fi done echo "✅ All required commands available." # Check and install Pillow for image compression echo "🐍 Checking Python dependencies..." if ! python3 -c "from PIL import Image" 2>/dev/null; then echo "📦 Installing Pillow for image compression..." echo " Run: sudo pacman -S python-pillow" sudo pacman -S --noconfirm python-pillow echo "✅ Pillow installed." else echo "✅ Pillow already installed." fi # ============================================================================= # Step 1: Initialize Git if needed # ============================================================================= if [ ! -d ".git" ]; then echo "📁 Initializing Git repository..." git init git remote add origin $MYREPO else echo "✅ Git repository already initialized." if ! git remote | grep -q 'origin'; then echo "🔗 Adding remote origin..." git remote add origin $MYREPO fi fi # ============================================================================= # Step 2: Sync posts from Obsidian to Hugo # ============================================================================= echo "📝 Syncing posts from Obsidian..." if [ ! -d "$OBSIDIAN_POSTS" ]; then echo "❌ Source path does not exist: $OBSIDIAN_POSTS" exit 1 fi if [ ! -d "$HUGO_POSTS" ]; then echo "📁 Creating destination path: $HUGO_POSTS" mkdir -p "$HUGO_POSTS" fi # Sync posts (trailing slash on source copies contents, not the folder itself) rsync -av --delete "$OBSIDIAN_POSTS/" "$HUGO_POSTS/" echo "✅ Posts synced." # ============================================================================= # Step 3: Sync attachments/images from Obsidian to Hugo # ============================================================================= echo "🖼️ Syncing images from Obsidian..." if [ ! -d "$OBSIDIAN_ATTACHMENTS" ]; then echo "⚠️ Attachments path does not exist: $OBSIDIAN_ATTACHMENTS" echo " Skipping image sync..." else if [ ! -d "$HUGO_IMAGES" ]; then echo "📁 Creating images directory: $HUGO_IMAGES" mkdir -p "$HUGO_IMAGES" fi rsync -av --delete "$OBSIDIAN_ATTACHMENTS/" "$HUGO_IMAGES/" echo "✅ Images synced." fi # ============================================================================= # Step 4: Compress images and convert Obsidian image links # ============================================================================= echo "🔄 Processing and compressing images..." python3 << 'PYTHON_SCRIPT' """ 1. Compress images in static/images (PNG/JPG) 2. Convert Obsidian image links to Hugo format """ import os import re from pathlib import Path # Try to import Pillow for image compression try: from PIL import Image PILLOW_AVAILABLE = True except ImportError: PILLOW_AVAILABLE = False print("⚠️ Pillow not installed. Skipping image compression.") print(" Install with: pip install Pillow") # ============================================================================= # Image Compression # ============================================================================= def compress_images(images_dir, max_width=1200, quality=85): """Compress images to reduce file size.""" if not PILLOW_AVAILABLE: return images_path = Path(images_dir) if not images_path.exists(): return image_extensions = {'.png', '.jpg', '.jpeg', '.webp'} image_files = [f for f in images_path.iterdir() if f.suffix.lower() in image_extensions] if not image_files: print("No images to compress.") return print(f"Compressing {len(image_files)} image(s)...") for img_path in image_files: try: original_size = img_path.stat().st_size with Image.open(img_path) as img: # Convert RGBA to RGB for JPEG (remove alpha channel) if img.mode == 'RGBA' and img_path.suffix.lower() in {'.jpg', '.jpeg'}: img = img.convert('RGB') # Resize if wider than max_width if img.width > max_width: ratio = max_width / img.width new_height = int(img.height * ratio) img = img.resize((max_width, new_height), Image.Resampling.LANCZOS) # Save with compression if img_path.suffix.lower() == '.png': img.save(img_path, 'PNG', optimize=True) elif img_path.suffix.lower() in {'.jpg', '.jpeg'}: img.save(img_path, 'JPEG', quality=quality, optimize=True) elif img_path.suffix.lower() == '.webp': img.save(img_path, 'WEBP', quality=quality) new_size = img_path.stat().st_size savings = ((original_size - new_size) / original_size) * 100 if savings > 0: print(f" ✅ {img_path.name}: {original_size//1024}KB → {new_size//1024}KB ({savings:.1f}% smaller)") else: print(f" ℹ️ {img_path.name}: already optimized") except Exception as e: print(f" ❌ Error compressing {img_path.name}: {e}") # ============================================================================= # Convert Obsidian Image Links # ============================================================================= def convert_obsidian_images(content): import urllib.parse pattern = r'!\[\[([^\]|]+)(?:\|([^\]]+))?\]\]' def replace_image(match): filepath = match.group(1).strip() alt_text = match.group(2) filename = os.path.basename(filepath) alt = alt_text.strip() if alt_text else os.path.splitext(filename)[0] # URL-encode the filename to handle spaces and special characters encoded_filename = urllib.parse.quote(filename) return f'![{alt}](/images/{encoded_filename})' return re.sub(pattern, replace_image, content) # ============================================================================= # Main # ============================================================================= # Compress images compress_images('/home/ozy/git/hugo-blog/static/images') # Process markdown files posts_dir = Path('/home/ozy/git/hugo-blog/content/blog') md_files = list(posts_dir.glob('**/*.md')) print(f"\nProcessing {len(md_files)} markdown file(s)...") for md_file in md_files: try: content = md_file.read_text(encoding='utf-8') if '![[' in content: new_content = convert_obsidian_images(content) if content != new_content: md_file.write_text(new_content, encoding='utf-8') print(f" ✅ Converted links: {md_file.name}") else: print(f" ℹ️ No changes: {md_file.name}") else: print(f" ⏭️ Skipped: {md_file.name}") except Exception as e: print(f" ❌ Error: {md_file.name}: {e}") print("Done.") PYTHON_SCRIPT echo "✅ Images processed." # ============================================================================= # Step 5: Build the Hugo site # ============================================================================= echo "🏗️ Building the Hugo site..." if ! hugo; then echo "❌ Hugo build failed." exit 1 fi echo "✅ Hugo site built." # ============================================================================= # Step 6: Stage changes for Git # ============================================================================= echo "📦 Staging changes for Git..." if git diff --quiet && git diff --cached --quiet; then echo "ℹ️ No changes to stage." else if [ "$DRY_RUN" = true ]; then echo "🔍 [DRY-RUN] Would stage changes:" git status --short else git add . echo "✅ Changes staged." fi fi # ============================================================================= # Step 7: Commit changes # ============================================================================= commit_message="New Blog Post on $(date +'%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S')" if [ "$DRY_RUN" = true ]; then if ! git diff --quiet; then echo "🔍 [DRY-RUN] Would commit with message: $commit_message" fi elif git diff --cached --quiet; then echo "ℹ️ No changes to commit." else echo "💾 Committing changes..." git commit -m "$commit_message" echo "✅ Changes committed." fi # ============================================================================= # Step 8: Push to branch # ============================================================================= if [ "$DRY_RUN" = true ]; then echo "🔍 [DRY-RUN] Would push to $BRANCH branch" else echo "🚀 Deploying to GitHub ($BRANCH)..." if ! git push origin "$BRANCH"; then echo "❌ Failed to push to $BRANCH branch." exit 1 fi echo "✅ Pushed to $BRANCH branch." fi # ============================================================================= # Done! # ============================================================================= echo "" if [ "$DRY_RUN" = true ]; then echo "🏁 Dry-run complete! No changes were committed or pushed." else echo "🎉 All done! Site synced, processed, committed, built, and pushed to $BRANCH." fi
summary: Using HUGO to deploy my personal note from obsidian (a markdown note app)
title: Moving my personal website to Hugo

EC2 server is virtual machine which running on hypervisor under AWS hardware. The new generation EC2 service is nitro based instance which require some configuration. In this tutorial I will go through all the requirement that you need to check or do.
Before starting this tutorial please see the following information from AWS doc regarding AWS Nitro System
The AWS Nitro System is the underlying platform for our next generation of EC2 instances that enables AWS to innovate faster, further reduce cost for our customers, and deliver added benefits like increased security and new instance types.
AWS has completely re-imagined our virtualization infrastructure. Traditionally, hypervisors protect the physical hardware and bios, virtualize the CPU, storage, networking, and provide a rich set of management capabilities. With the Nitro System, we are able to break apart those functions, offload them to dedicated hardware and software, and reduce costs by delivering practically all of the resources of a server to your instances.
Most of problem when changing instance type to nitro base support is the nitro base instance require ENA-attribute enabled, ENA module and NVME module installed on the instance and will cause failing status check if we force change the instance type without enabling ENA-attribute and the installing the module.
prerequisites: basic understanding of AWS EC2 service, AWS CLI and Linux bash command.
Steps on how to resize AWS nitro-based instance type: Create an Image of the current system Download the nitro instance check script and running it Check the ENA-attribute support is enable on your instance Resize your instance type to M5 Start the instance and check if the instance up and running with status check 2/2 Create the AMI of the current system By creating the AMI we can do a rollback if the changes that we made is not working as we expect. You can put the Image name and description and go ahead to create the Image. It will take a few minutes depends on the size of EBS volume attached to the instance.
Download and Run the NitroInstanceChecks script See the following description from AWS doc on what the script do:
The NitroInstanceChecks script checks your instance and provides a pass/fail status of these requirements:
Verifies if the NVMe module is installed on your instance. If yes, then the script verifies that the module is loaded in the initramfs image. Verifies if the ENA module is installed on your instance. Analyzes /etc/fstab and looks for block devices being mounted using device names. This script is supported on the following OS versions:
Red Hat derivatives: Red Hat Linux, Red Hat Enterprise Linux, CentOS Amazon Linux, Amazon Linux 2 Debian derivatives: Debian, Ubuntu You can download the script in this repository:
https://github.com/awslabs/aws-support-tools/tree/master/EC2/NitroInstanceChecks
Download the script curl -o nitro_check_script.sh https://raw.githubusercontent.com/awslabs/aws-support-tools/master/EC2/NitroInstanceChecks/nitro_check_script.sh Make the script executable chmod +x nitro_check_script.sh Execute the script sudo ./nitro_check_script.sh Check the ENA-attribute support is enable on your instance aws ec2 describe-instances --instance-ids ${INSTANCE_ID} --query "Reservations[].Instances[].EnaSupport" If you get empty response ([ ]) then it means it’s not enabled.
Please use the following command to stop the instance and enable ena-support using AWS CLI
aws ec2 stop-instances --instance-id ${INSTANCE_ID} aws ec2 modify-instance-attribute --instance-id ${INSTANCE_ID} --ena-support If you get response ([true]) it means the instance already ENA enabled and you can go ahead resize the instance.
Resize your instance type to M5 Stop your instance and resize it from M4 to M5 using AWS cli
aws ec2 stop-instances --instance-id ${INSTANCE_ID} aws ec2 modify-instance-attribute --instance-id ${INSTANCE_ID} --instance-type '{"Value": "m5a.2xlarge"}' Start the instance and check if the instance up and running with status check 2/2 aws ec2 start-instances --instance-id ${INSTANCE_ID} reference: https://aws.amazon.com/premiumsupport/knowledge-center/boot-error-linux-nitro-instance/
summary: The new generation EC2 service is nitro based instance which require some configuration. In this tutorial I will go through all the requirement that you need to check or do.
title: How to Resize AWS Nitro-based Instance Type — Use Case M4-M5
